claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from tumor studies.

claims.claim: NK cells recruited to tumors are engaged by RAE-1ε induced on endothelial cells in the tumor microenvironment.
claims.source: These data are consistent with a model in which NK cells recruited to tumors are engaged by RAE-1ε induced on endothelial cells in the tumor microenvironment.
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: NKG2D-KO mice showed reduced and delayed mortality compared with matched WT controls when challenged with B16 cells intravenously.
claims.source: WT and NKG2D-KO mice were injected intravenously with a limiting number of B16 cells and monitored for survival. Consistent with our hypothesis, NKG2D-KO mice showed reduced and delayed mortality compared with matched WT controls (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: NK depletion resulted in dramatically accelerated mortality in WT and NKG2D-KO mice challenged with B16 cells, eliminating the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency.
claims.source: Importantly, NK depletion resulted in dramatically accelerated mortality in WT and NKG2D-KO mice, eliminating the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency.
claims.evidence: Supported by survival data from NK-depleted mice.

claims.claim: NKG2D-KO mice were more capable of controlling B16 tumor growth than WT counterparts when implanted subcutaneously.
claims.source: When WT or NKG2D-KO mice were implanted with B16 cells subcutaneously, NKG2D-KO mice were more capable of controlling B16 tumor growth than WT counterparts (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Rag2/NKG2D double knockout mice resisted B16 tumors better than Rag2-KO mice.
claims.source: We also found that Rag2/NKG2D double knockout mice resisted B16 tumors better than Rag2-KO mice, indicating that T cells (and B cells) are not required for the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: T cells (and B cells) are not required for the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency against B16 tumors.
claims.source: We also found that Rag2/NKG2D double knockout mice resisted B16 tumors better than Rag2-KO mice, indicating that T cells (and B cells) are not required for the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the protective effect persists in Rag2-KO background.

claims.claim: Treatment of NKG2D-WT mice with anti-NKG2D antibody in vivo starting the day before tumor cell implantation resulted in enhanced control of B16 tumors comparable to the NKG2D-KO mice.
claims.source: A subsequent experiment on the Rag2-KO background showed that treatment of NKG2D-WT mice with anti-NKG2D antibody in vivo starting the day before tumor cell implantation resulted in enhanced control of B16 tumors comparable to the NKG2D-KO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: NKG2D-KO mice showed better control of subcutaneous RMA-S tumors than did their WT counterparts.
claims.source: We then turned to the RMA-S lymphoma transplant tumor model, which is targeted in vivo by NK cells through 'missing self' recognition but also does not express NKG2D ligands. NKG2D-KO mice showed better control of subcutaneous RMA-S tumors than did their WT counterparts (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: NKG2D expression mitigates in vivo NK responses to tumors that lack NKG2D ligands.
claims.source: These data indicate that NKG2D expression mitigates in vivo NK responses to tumors that lack NKG2D ligands, and that this desensitizing effect is reversed by acute antibody blockade of NKG2D.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the tumor challenge experiments.

claims.claim: The desensitizing effect of NKG2D is reversed by acute antibody blockade of NKG2D.
claims.source: These data indicate that NKG2D expression mitigates in vivo NK responses to tumors that lack NKG2D ligands, and that this desensitizing effect is reversed by acute antibody blockade of NKG2D.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the tumor challenge experiments with antibody blockade.

claims.claim: The growth of B16-MULT1 tumors was accelerated in NKG2D-KO mice compared with WT controls.
claims.source: Despite the NK hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-deficient animals, NKG2D-KO NK cells cannot recognize MULT1, and the growth of B16-MULT1 tumors was accelerated in NKG2D-KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: NKG2D-KO NK cells cannot recognize MULT1.
claims.source: Despite the NK hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-deficient animals, NKG2D-KO NK cells cannot recognize MULT1, and the growth of B16-MULT1 tumors was accelerated in NKG2D-KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about NKG2D-KO NK cells.

claims.claim: NKG2D interactions with tumor NKG2D ligands have a strong protective role.
claims.source: These data are consistent with previous studies showing a strong protective role for NKG2D interactions with tumor NKG2D ligands (Cerwenka et al., 2001; Diefenbach et al., 2001; Guerra et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: RAE-1-KO mice challenged with B16-MULT1 tumors exhibited superior tumor rejection compared with WT mice.
claims.source: Indeed, RAE-1-KO mice challenged with B16-MULT1 tumors exhibited superior tumor rejection compared with WT mice (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: TRAMP-C2 cells express RAE-1δ and RAE-1ε and are sensitive to NK cells.
claims.source: We then turned to a transplant tumor model with endogenous NKG2D ligand expression, the TRAMP-C2 model of prostate adenocarcinoma. TRAMP-C2 cells express RAE-1δ and RAE-1ε and are sensitive to NK cells, and this sensitivity is partly dependent on NKG2D (Jamieson et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: TRAMP-C2 cell sensitivity to NK cells is partly dependent on NKG2D.
claims.source: We then turned to a transplant tumor model with endogenous NKG2D ligand expression, the TRAMP-C2 model of prostate adenocarcinoma. TRAMP-C2 cells express RAE-1δ and RAE-1ε and are sensitive to NK cells, and this sensitivity is partly dependent on NKG2D (Jamieson et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: RAE-1-KO mice showed enhanced control of TRAMP-C2 tumors compared with WT controls.
claims.source: When injected subcutaneously into WT and RAE-1-KO mice, the RAE-1-KO mice showed enhanced control of TRAMP-C2 tumors compared with WT controls (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Interactions between NKG2D and endogenous RAE-1ε desensitize NK responses to tumors in vivo.
claims.source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that interactions between NKG2D and endogenous RAE-1ε desensitize NK responses to tumors in vivo, whereas NKG2D ligands expressed on tumor cells promote antitumor NK responses.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the tumor challenge experiments.

claims.claim: NKG2D ligands expressed on tumor cells promote antitumor NK responses.
claims.source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that interactions between NKG2D and endogenous RAE-1ε desensitize NK responses to tumors in vivo, whereas NKG2D ligands expressed on tumor cells promote antitumor NK responses.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the tumor challenge experiments.

claims.claim: NKG2D is engaged by endogenous RAE-1ε in healthy WT mice, causing constitutive downregulation of NKG2D from the NK cell surface.
claims.source: We show that the activating receptor NKG2D is engaged by endogenous RAE-1ε in healthy WT mice, causing constitutive downregulation of NKG2D from the NK cell surface, and leads to an intrinsic global desensitization of NK cells to acute stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: NKG2D engagement by endogenous RAE-1ε leads to an intrinsic global desensitization of NK cells to acute stimulation.
claims.source: We show that the activating receptor NKG2D is engaged by endogenous RAE-1ε in healthy WT mice, causing constitutive downregulation of NKG2D from the NK cell surface, and leads to an intrinsic global desensitization of NK cells to acute stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: Preventing NKG2D interactions with host RAE-1ε enhanced NK cell antitumor responses in vivo.
claims.source: Moreover, preventing NKG2D interactions with host RAE-1ε enhanced NK cell antitumor responses in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: Endothelial cells were found to express RAE-1ε constitutively in lymph nodes.
claims.source: Bone marrow chimera experiments identified nonhematopoietic cells as the dominant source of RAE-1ε, and endothelial cells were found to express RAE-1ε constitutively in lymph nodes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: RAE-1ε expression on tumor-associated endothelial cells was super-induced compared to endothelial cells in lymph nodes.
claims.source: In tumors, RAE-1ε expression on tumor-associated endothelial cells was super-induced compared to endothelial cells in lymph nodes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: Endothelial RAE-1ε interacts with NKG2D to desensitize NK cells and diminish antitumor NK responses.
claims.source: These data support a model in which endothelial RAE-1ε interacts with NKG2D to desensitize NK cells and diminish antitumor NK responses.
claims.evidence: This is a summary model based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: NK cell hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-KO mice has been reported previously by several groups.
claims.source: NK cell hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-KO mice has been reported previously by several groups including ours (Zafirova et al., 2009; Sheppard et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2015), although the trend of increased responsiveness did not reach statistical significance in our original characterization of the NKG2D-KO mouse (Guerra et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: NKG2D can participate in immune surveillance of cancer by recognizing NKG2D ligands on tumor cells to induce NK cell activation and tumor cell killing.
claims.source: At the same time, our results support the classical view that NKG2D can participate in immune surveillance of cancer by recognizing NKG2D ligands on tumor cells to induce NK cell activation and tumor cell killing (Diefenbach et al., 2000; Cerwenka et al., 2001; Diefenbach et al., 2001; Jamieson et al., 2002; Guerra et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: NKG2D confers opposing effects, both promoting killing of tumor cells that express NKG2D ligands, and desensitizing NK cells through interactions with host ligands.
claims.source: Hence, NKG2D confers opposing effects, both promoting killing of tumor cells that express NKG2D ligands, and desensitizing NK cells through interactions with host ligands.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The net outcome of NKG2D's opposing effects depends on the complement of NK-activating ligands that a given tumor cell expresses, among other factors.
claims.source: We propose that the net outcome of these opposing effects of NKG2D depends on the complement of NK-activating ligands that a given tumor cell expresses, among other factors.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: For tumor cells that express abundant NKG2D ligands, the ability of NKG2D to promote acute activation against the tumor can outweigh the opposing desensitizing interactions with host cells.
claims.source: For tumor cells that express abundant NKG2D ligands, the ability of NKG2D to promote acute activation against the tumor can outweigh the opposing desensitizing interactions with host cells.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Loss of NKG2D results in reduced tumor killing of B16-MULT1 tumors and YAC-1 cells.
claims.source: In this circumstance, loss of NKG2D results in reduced tumor killing, as exemplified by the observation that NKG2D-deficient mice show reduced killing/rejection of B16-MULT1 tumors and YAC-1 cells (Figure 6D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Jamieson et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to published literature.

claims.claim: NKG2D-KO mice were defective in immune surveillance of spontaneous tumors that express NKG2D ligands, such as prostate adenocarcinomas in TRAMP mice and lymphomas in Eu-Myc mice.
claims.source: We speculate that this situation also applies to previous findings that NKG2D-KO mice were defective in immune surveillance of spontaneous tumors that express NKG2D ligands, such as prostate adenocarcinomas in TRAMP mice and lymphomas in Eu-Myc mice (Guerra et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on previous findings cited from published literature.

claims.claim: For tumor cells that express abundant other NK-activating ligands and either do not express NKG2D ligands or depend little on NKG2D ligands for NK killing, the global desensitization of NK cells caused by NKG2D interactions with host ligands is predicted to exert a dominant effect.

results.result: NKG2D is constitutively engaged by endogenous RAE-1ε in healthy WT mice, causing internalization of NKG2D from the NK cell surface. RAE-1ε is expressed constitutively by lymph node endothelial cells and highly induced on tumor-associated endothelium. Antibody blockade of RAE-1ε or genetic deletion of RAE-1 increases NKG2D surface levels on NK cells as early as 12 hours, without affecting NKG2D mRNA levels, indicating post-translational regulation through receptor internalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C37-C50 are strongly supported by multiple complementary experimental approaches including antibody blockade (C37-C39), genetic knockout (C40-C43), mRNA analysis (C43-C44), and adoptive transfer experiments (C48-C49). The data consistently demonstrate RAE-1ε-mediated NKG2D downregulation across multiple tissues. The conclusion that internalization is the mechanism (C44) is appropriately inferred from unchanged mRNA levels with altered surface protein.

results.result: Endogenous RAE-1ε-NKG2D interaction desensitizes NK cell responses globally to acute stimulation through multiple activating receptors. NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice show significantly enhanced degranulation and IFNγ production when stimulated through NKp46, NK1.1, or NKG2D itself, with particularly marked effects in peritoneal NK cells. Similar hyper-responsiveness is observed after antibody blockade of RAE-1ε as early as 48 hours, and RAE-1-KO NK cells show enhanced killing of YAC-1 tumor cells in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C54-C63 are well-supported by functional assays showing consistent hyper-responsiveness of RAE-1-KO NK cells across multiple stimulation conditions (C54-C58) and enhanced cytotoxicity (C62). The global desensitization effect is demonstrated by elevated responses through multiple distinct receptors (NKp46, NK1.1, NKG2D), not just NKG2D itself. The kinetics are established by time-course experiments (C59).

results.result: NKG2D desensitizes NK responses in a cell-intrinsic manner, and NKG2D-KO NK cells are even more hyper-responsive than RAE-1-KO NK cells. Mixed bone marrow chimeras containing both WT and NKG2D-KO NK cells in the same animal show that NKG2D-KO NK cells remain hyper-responsive compared to WT NK cells, demonstrating cell-intrinsic regulation. The greater responsiveness of NKG2D-KO versus RAE-1-KO NK cells suggests additional ligands or ligand-independent mechanisms contribute to NKG2D-mediated desensitization.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are strongly supported by mixed bone marrow chimera experiments (C69) that definitively demonstrate cell-intrinsic effects by comparing WT and NKG2D-KO NK cells within the same host environment. The observation that NKG2D-KO NK cells are more responsive than RAE-1-KO NK cells (C67) is consistently shown and appropriately interpreted as suggesting additional mechanisms (C68), though this remains speculative.

results.result: Nonhematopoietic cells are the dominant source of RAE-1ε responsible for NKG2D engagement and NK desensitization. Bone marrow chimera experiments show that mice with RAE-1ε restricted to nonhematopoietic cells (KO→WT) completely recapitulate low NKG2D levels and desensitized NK responses seen in WT→WT controls, while mice with RAE-1ε only in hematopoietic cells (WT→KO) show high NKG2D levels comparable to KO→KO chimeras. Similar patterns are observed in tumor microenvironments.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76, C83, C91, C98 are well-supported by systematic bone marrow chimera experiments that isolate the contribution of hematopoietic versus nonhematopoietic RAE-1ε. The data consistently show dominant effects of nonhematopoietic RAE-1ε on both NKG2D surface levels (C71-C73) and functional NK responses (C74-C75). The radiation dose used (600+500 Gy) achieves >99% reconstitution, though radio-resistant cells cannot be completely excluded.

results.result: Endothelial cells in secondary lymphoid organs constitutively express RAE-1ε at steady state, with particularly high expression on high endothelial venules (HEVs). Blood endothelial cells (BECs) and lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) in inguinal lymph nodes show substantial RAE-1ε expression, while fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs) and double-negative (DN) cells show little to no expression. Endothelium in lung, liver, and heart shows minimal RAE-1ε, suggesting tissue-specific regulation by the lymphoid microenvironment.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82, C84, C122, C142-C144 are strongly supported by flow cytometry analysis of dissociated lymph nodes identifying RAE-1ε on specific stromal populations. Antibody specificity is confirmed using RAE-1-KO mice as negative controls (C79). The tissue-specific expression pattern (C80-C81, C143) and particularly high expression on HEVs (C82) are clearly demonstrated. However, the authors appropriately acknowledge (C147) that endothelial-specific RAE-1ε-KO mice would be needed for definitive proof.

results.result: Tumor-associated endothelial cells express especially high levels of RAE-1ε compared to lymph node endothelium, and this endothelial RAE-1ε engages NKG2D on tumor-infiltrating NK cells. RAE-1ε blockade or RAE-1 deficiency increases NKG2D levels on tumor-infiltrating NK cells in B16 and RMA-S tumors that lack NKG2D ligand expression. High endothelial RAE-1ε expression is observed across multiple tumor models including transplanted melanoma, lymphoma, prostate cancer, and autochthonous KP sarcomas, with levels exceeding those on lymph node endothelium.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C99, C123, C151-C152 are well-supported by flow cytometry analysis of tumor-infiltrating NK cells and tumor-associated endothelial cells across multiple tumor models. The use of B16 and RMA-S tumors that lack NKG2D ligands (C86, C90) provides strong evidence that endogenous host RAE-1ε, not tumor-expressed ligands, is responsible for NKG2D downregulation. The super-induction on tumor endothelium compared to lymph nodes (C93, C152) is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Preventing NKG2D interactions with endogenous RAE-1ε enhances NK antitumor responses in vivo against tumors lacking NKG2D ligands. NKG2D-KO mice show reduced mortality and better tumor control than WT mice when challenged with B16 melanoma or RMA-S lymphoma cells that do not express NKG2D ligands. The protective effect is NK-dependent, as NK depletion eliminates the survival advantage. Similar protection is observed with antibody blockade of NKG2D and in Rag2/NKG2D double knockout mice, indicating T and B cells are not required.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C109, C117, C121 are strongly supported by multiple in vivo tumor challenge experiments using different models (i.v. and s.c. B16, RMA-S) and approaches (genetic knockout, antibody blockade). The NK-dependence is definitively shown by NK depletion experiments (C102). The use of tumors lacking NKG2D ligands (B16, RMA-S) is critical for isolating the desensitizing effect of host RAE-1ε from activating effects of tumor-expressed ligands.

results.result: NKG2D has opposing effects on tumor immunity: it promotes killing of tumor cells expressing NKG2D ligands while desensitizing NK cells through interactions with host ligands. NKG2D-KO mice show accelerated growth of B16-MULT1 tumors expressing the NKG2D ligand MULT1, demonstrating the importance of NKG2D-mediated tumor recognition. Conversely, RAE-1-KO mice show enhanced rejection of both B16-MULT1 and TRAMP-C2 tumors that express NKG2D ligands, indicating that eliminating host RAE-1ε enhances NK responses even when tumor cells express NKG2D ligands.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113, C116, C118, C127-C128, C131 are well-supported by tumor challenge experiments comparing responses to NKG2D ligand-positive versus ligand-negative tumors. The opposing effects are clearly demonstrated: NKG2D-KO mice are protected from ligand-negative tumors (C101-C107) but show worse outcomes with ligand-positive tumors (C110). The enhanced rejection of ligand-positive tumors in RAE-1-KO mice (C113, C116) demonstrates that the desensitizing effect of host RAE-1ε can be overcome when tumors express sufficient NKG2D ligands.

results.result: Endogenous RAE-1ε plays a significant but not complete role in NKG2D-mediated NK desensitization. NK cells from NKG2D-KO mice consistently show greater responsiveness than NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice when stimulated through NKp46, suggesting additional NKG2D ligands or ligand-independent mechanisms contribute to desensitization. The authors acknowledge that other mechanisms such as interactions with other ligands at steady state or tonic signaling through NKG2D may contribute.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140, C68 are supported by direct comparison of RAE-1-KO and NKG2D-KO NK cell responses (C67, C138). The observation that NKG2D-KO cells are more responsive than RAE-1-KO cells is consistent across experiments. The authors appropriately interpret this as suggesting additional mechanisms (C68, C140) while acknowledging these remain speculative. The data clearly support that RAE-1ε is important but not the sole mechanism.

results.result: Splenic NK cell numbers and maturation markers are similar in WT and RAE-1-KO mice. Flow cytometry analysis shows comparable NK cell frequencies and expression of CD11b and CD27 maturation markers between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by flow cytometry data showing no significant differences in NK cell numbers or maturation markers. This is an important control demonstrating that the functional differences observed are not due to altered NK development or maturation. The citation supporting CD11b/CD27 as maturation markers (C53) is appropriate.

results.result: RAE-1-KO mice were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 to introduce frameshift mutations in both Raet1d and Raet1e genes. NKG2D-mediated recognition is required for efficient killing of YAC-1 tumor cells, as NKG2D-KO NK cells show significantly reduced YAC-1 killing while RAE-1-KO NK cells show enhanced killing.
results.evaluation: Claims C40, C60-C61 are supported by citation to the published generation of RAE-1-KO mice (C40) and in vitro cytotoxicity assays (C60). The differential killing of YAC-1 cells by NKG2D-KO versus RAE-1-KO NK cells provides important validation that the hyper-responsiveness of RAE-1-KO cells translates to enhanced tumor killing. The requirement for NKG2D in YAC-1 killing is consistent with published literature (C61).

results.result: Background on NK cell biology, desensitization mechanisms, and NKG2D. NK cells recognize unhealthy cells using activating and inhibitory receptors, with responsiveness dynamically tuned by steady-state receptor-ligand interactions. MHC I-Ly49 interactions are well-established regulators of NK responsiveness, while the endogenous activating receptor-ligand systems remain incompletely defined. NKG2D is an activating receptor that binds diverse MHC-like ligands and has been implicated in NK desensitization based on prior studies showing hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C36 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These claims establish the scientific context for the current study and are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made. Claim C18 appropriately identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

results.result: Proposed model: NK cells trafficking through lymphoid tissue during homeostatic circulation are continuously engaged and desensitized by RAE-1ε expressed on endothelial cells, and NK cells recruited to tumors are engaged by RAE-1ε induced on tumor-associated endothelium. The specific expression on lymphoid endothelium suggests the system may be designed to desensitize NK cells traversing this tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C85, C100, C124, C145 represent proposed models and speculation based on the experimental findings. While the underlying data supporting these models are sound (endothelial RAE-1ε expression, NK desensitization), the specific mechanisms of how NK cells encounter endothelial RAE-1ε during circulation and the teleological interpretation (C145) remain speculative. The authors appropriately present these as models/suggestions rather than proven mechanisms.

results.result: Discussion of NKG2D's dual role and context-dependence. The authors discuss how the net outcome of NKG2D's opposing effects depends on tumor cell ligand expression and microenvironmental context, reconciling their findings with prior literature showing both protective and detrimental roles for NKG2D in different tumor models.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C137 provide appropriate discussion contextualizing the current findings within prior literature.
